section.title: Into Your Hands I Commit My Spirit
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of David combining urgent lament with settled trust, its central confession, 'Into Your hands I commit my spirit,' becoming the very words Jesus prayed from the cross, Luke 23:46. David's distress, betrayal by friends, and grief give way to praise for God's goodness and a closing call to be strong and take heart.
section.thesis: David commits his life into God's hands amid betrayal, grief, and mortal danger, and that same confession becomes the dying prayer of Jesus Christ, who entrusted His spirit to the Father and was raised in vindication of that trust.
section.frameNote: Five movements: trust and the commit of his spirit into God's hands (1-5); continued confidence and rejection of worthless idols (6-8); distress, grief, and betrayal by friends (9-13); renewed trust despite distress and prayer against the wicked (14-18); and praise for God's goodness, closing with a call to be strong and take heart (19-24).

units.label: Into Your hands I commit my spirit
units.note: trust and the commit of his spirit

verses.text:
In You, O LORD, I have {{chasah|taken refuge}}; let me never be put to shame; 
save me by Your righteousness.
Incline Your ear to me; come quickly to my rescue. Be my rock of refuge, the stronghold of my deliverance.
For You are my rock and my fortress; lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name.
You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge.
Into Your hands I commit my {{ruach|spirit}}; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of {{emet|truth}}.
I hate those who cling to worthless idols, but in the LORD I trust.

I will be glad and rejoice in Your loving devotion, for You have seen my affliction; 
You have known the anguish of my soul.
You have not delivered me to the enemy; You have set my feet in the open.

units.label: I am dreaded by my friends

verses.text: Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eyes fail from sorrow, my soul and body as well.
For my life is consumed with grief and my years with groaning; my iniquity has drained my strength, and my bones are wasting away.
Among all my enemies I am a disgrace, and among my neighbors even more. I am dreaded by my friends, they flee when they see me on the street.
I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind. I am like a broken vessel.
For I hear the slander of many; there is terror on every side. They conspire against me and plot to take my life.

units.label: My times are in Your hands

verses.text: But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, "You are my God."

My times are in Your hands; deliver me from my enemies 
and from those who pursue me.
Make Your face shine on Your servant; save me by Your loving devotion.
O LORD, let me not be ashamed, for I have called on You. Let the wicked be put to shame; let them lie silent in Sheol.

May lying lips be silenced, lips that speak with arrogance against the righteous, 
full of pride and contempt.

units.label: Blessed be the LORD
units.note: praise and a closing call to courage

verses.text: How great is Your goodness which You have laid up for those who fear You, which You have bestowed before the sons of men on those who take refuge in You!
You hide them in the secret place of Your presence from the schemes of men. You conceal them in Your shelter from accusing tongues.

Blessed be the LORD, for He has shown me His loving devotion 
in a city under siege.
In my alarm I said, "I am cut off from Your sight!" But You heard my plea for mercy when I called to You for help.

Love the LORD, all His saints. The LORD preserves the faithful, 
but fully repays the arrogant.
Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD.

chasah.gloss: To take refuge, seek shelter, as a bird under wings or a traveler in a fortress. It describes an active, ongoing trust rather than a single act, the posture David maintains throughout the psalm even amid betrayal and danger.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, the animating life given by God. David commits this very spirit into God's hands, words that become the dying prayer of Jesus on the cross, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit,' Luke 23:46.

emet.gloss: Truth, faithfulness, reliability. David appeals to God as the God of emet, whose redemption can be trusted absolutely, the same faithfulness fully displayed when God raised Jesus from the dead in vindication of His trust.

basic.context: David takes refuge in the LORD as rock and fortress, committing his very spirit into God's hands, confident in the God of truth who redeems him. Yet the psalm turns to raw distress: grief, physical wasting, disgrace before enemies and neighbors, and even dread among his own friends who flee at the sight of him. He renews his trust, declaring that his times are in God's hands, prays against lying and arrogant accusers, and closes in praise for God's goodness hidden away for those who take refuge in Him, urging all who hope in the LORD to be strong and courageous.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should be read as an integrated whole in which trust does not eliminate grief but is proven precisely in the middle of betrayal and distress; its central confession, verse 5, carries weight far beyond David's own life because Jesus Himself prayed these very words while dying.
basic.originalLanguages: David has chasah, taken refuge, in the LORD, an ongoing posture rather than a single decision, and commits his ruach, spirit, into God's hands, appealing to Him as the God of emet, truth and faithfulness, whose redemption can be utterly relied upon even at the point of death.
basic.typology: David's commitment of his spirit into God's hands, verse 5, becomes, without alteration, the dying words of Jesus on the cross, Luke 23:46, and David's experience of being forgotten like a dead man and like a broken vessel, verse 12, anticipates the humiliation and apparent abandonment of the suffering Messiah, who was nonetheless vindicated by resurrection.
basic.christ: Jesus prays this psalm's central verse word for word as He dies: 'Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit,' Luke 23:46, taking up David's confession of trust as His own final act of faith before death. Where David was delivered from death's threat, Jesus actually died and was raised, the God of emet, truth, proving faithful not merely to preserve life but to conquer death itself, vindicating every word of trust this psalm contains, Acts 2:24.
basic.god: God is shown as a faithful refuge who sees affliction, knows the anguish of the soul, and can be trusted utterly even at the point of death, His goodness hidden away like treasure for those who take refuge in Him and displayed openly before the world in due time.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 23:46 records Jesus praying the exact words of verse 5 as He dies on the cross, the ultimate fulfillment of this psalm's central trust. Acts 2:24 declares that God raised Jesus, freeing Him from the agony of death, because it was not possible for death to hold Him, the vindication of trust this psalm anticipates. Romans 8:31-39 echoes this psalm's confidence that nothing, not even death, can separate believers from the love of God found in Christ Jesus.
basic.oneStory: David's confession, 'Into Your hands I commit my spirit,' spoken amid grief, betrayal, and mortal danger, becomes the very prayer Jesus prays while dying on the cross, and just as David trusted the God of truth for redemption, the Father raised Jesus from the dead, proving that trust in God's hands is never in vain, even at the point of death.

context.literary:
The psalm moves in waves, and each wave repeats the same three beats: petition, complaint, trust. The first wave, verses 1 to 8, opens with a cluster of requests and images of safe places, ends with a declaration of thanks in advance, and closes on the phrase 'in the open'. The second wave, verses 9 to 18, plunges into the trouble, with the body, the neighbours and the conspirators each described in turn, and rises again at verse 14 with the great turn, 'But I trust in You'. The third wave, verses 19 to 24, is a hymn of wonder at hidden goodness, an account of an escape, and a summons to the congregation.

Two contrasting spaces give the poem its structure. The prayer begins with narrow places and refuges: a rock, a fortress, a net, a stronghold. It then moves to distress, which the Hebrew words picture as tightness, and ends with feet set in the open, verse 8, and a shelter or 'secret place' in verses 19 and 20. The man who pleads to be hidden in verse 1 is hidden in verse 20, but by God, in His own presence, and not by the walls he feared. The poem is a journey from being shut in by enemies to being sheltered by God.

The centre of the psalm lies in verses 14 and 15. 'I say, "You are my God"' is the confession on which the rest depends, and 'My times are in Your hands' is its meaning. The two verses stand at the exact turning point between the long complaint of verses 9 to 13 and the requests that follow.

The voice also shifts. It begins as a private prayer, moves to address the enemies' schemes, and then turns outward to 'all His saints' and 'all you who hope', verses 23 and 24. What David has learned in private is offered as a public charge. The last two verses are addressed to a crowd, and they turn a lament into a liturgy.
context.historical:
The heading names David and gives the psalm to the choirmaster, which means it was collected for use in the temple worship. It does not say when the trouble happened. Readers have set it in the flight from Saul, when David was hunted by the king he had served, or in the days of Absalom's revolt, when his own household turned on him. Some look at Keilah, where Saul thought he had trapped David 'by entering a town with gates and bars', 1 Samuel 23:7, and take the 'city under siege' of verse 21 as an echo of that place. The psalm does not say, and its lack of names has helped it be prayed by later people in later troubles.

What the psalm does show is the social world of a man in disgrace. In a culture built on honour and family, a man who suffered public trouble found his friends pulling away. Sickness, disgrace and slander went together, as the friends of Job show, and to be 'dreaded' by neighbours in verse 11 meant that people crossed the street lest they be tainted. The slander of verse 13 and the phrase 'terror on every side' belong to a period when accusation could be lethal. Jeremiah uses the same phrase of himself when his neighbours whisper against him, Jeremiah 20:10.

The opening lines of the psalm are almost the same as the opening of Psalm 71, 'In You, O LORD, I have taken refuge; let me never be put to shame', Psalm 71:1-3. Prayers of this type were evidently handed down and reused. The closing summons in verse 24 uses the language of the commissioning of Joshua, 'Be strong and courageous', Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:9. David is speaking to a people who remember how Israel was told to face the conquest of Canaan, and he applies the same charge to those facing any conflict at all.
context.canonical:
The psalm is quoted in the Bible's most solemn scene. On the cross Jesus cried, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit', Luke 23:46, taking up verse 5 and adding the word 'Father'. The Bible's footnote on Psalm 31:5 itself notes the citation. Stephen's dying prayer, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit', Acts 7:59, is a second echo, and 1 Peter 4:19 tells suffering believers to 'entrust their souls to their faithful Creator', drawing on the same idea. The psalm has therefore become a form of words for dying in trust, from Jesus to Stephen to ordinary believers.

Jeremiah is the psalm's closest prophetic relative. Its phrase 'terror on every side' appears in Jeremiah 6:25, 20:3 and 20:10, and the whisper of many against him in Jeremiah 20:10 sounds like verse 13. Both men prayed under conspiracy from those they trusted and both refused to give up trusting God. Lamentations 2:22 takes up the same phrase for a whole city under judgment. Jonah 2:8 repeats the words of verse 6 about those who cling to worthless idols, and sets them beside his own prayer from the fish.

The charge of verse 24 belongs with a chain of exhortations: Deuteronomy 31:6, Joshua 1:9, Psalm 27:14. The word 'hope' in the last line links the psalm to Psalm 33:18 and 33:22, the next but one in the collection.

In the New Testament the theme of goodness stored up for those who fear God finds its answer in the believer's inheritance 'reserved in heaven', 1 Peter 1:4, and in the life 'hidden with Christ in God', Colossians 3:3, which reads like a commentary on the 'secret place of Your presence' in verse 20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted to teach that faith is a discipline of holding on, not a feeling of ease. The psalm keeps trust and terror in the same lines, verses 14 and 22 for example, and it will not let the reader think that a person of faith is someone who never feels cut off. In verse 22 he says that in his alarm he said, 'I am cut off from Your sight!', and then admits that God heard his plea anyway. The verse is offered as a correction of his own hasty judgment: the feeling was not the fact.

He also wanted his hearers to see where safety comes from. He does not ask for his enemies to be fewer or his neighbours more kind. He asks to be hidden in God and then declares that he has been. The goodness that he praises is 'laid up', kept in store for those who fear God, and offered in the sight of people. The point is that faithfulness to the LORD will be visible in the end.

The psalm concludes as a charge to a congregation, which shows the purpose behind the whole poem. David had walked through slander, sickness and abandonment, and he wants every hearer who suffers the same to know that the road leads out into the open. The people who 'hope in the LORD' are told to be strong, and the reason is given in the preceding line: the LORD preserves the faithful.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes the experience of one person, and it includes statements that should not be applied as they stand. David says he hates those who cling to worthless idols, verse 6, and he asks that the wicked lie silent in Sheol, verse 17. These are the words of a man wronged, not a rule that every believer must hate people. The New Testament asks us to love enemies and to pray for them, Matthew 5:44, and the way Jesus prays this psalm on the cross, after first asking forgiveness for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34, shows how the two sit together.

What the psalm prescribes is a pattern of prayer in trouble. The believer takes refuge before rescue arrives, commits his life to God, describes his real condition without embellishment, states his trust aloud, and gives thanks in advance for what is stored up. It also makes verse 5 a model for facing death. The Lord Himself used it, and the church has used it since as a bedtime and deathbed prayer. When the psalm says 'my times are in Your hands', it is not a promise that the times will be easy, but a claim about who holds them.

debates.question: What does the psalmist mean by 'my iniquity has drained my strength' in verse 10?

views.label: He admits that his own sin has brought on the suffering
views.case: The word translated 'iniquity' is the ordinary Hebrew term for guilt or wrongdoing, and the psalm speaks of bones wasting away in much the same way as the confession psalm that follows it, Psalm 32:3-4. On this reading verse 10 is a confession that the trouble is partly deserved, and the trust of the other verses is trust in God's mercy, not in David's innocence.

views.label: The word refers to affliction, not to guilt
views.case: Some interpreters read the Hebrew word as 'affliction' or 'misery', since the psalm elsewhere protests that the enemies' slander is unjust and describes David's righteous cause, verse 1 and verse 18. Verse 10 would then belong to the complaint against those who wronged him.

views.label: Both are true at once
views.case: A sufferer can be innocent of the charges being made against him and yet know that he is a sinner before God. Psalm 130:3 and Psalm 143:2 hold the two together, and Job's friends err by insisting that one explanation must cover everything.

debates.bearing: The psalm gives no verdict, and nothing in it depends on one. If the suffering was deserved, God is still a refuge who redeems. If it was undeserved, God is still the one who sees affliction, verse 7. Either way, the answer to the trouble is the same: commit the spirit to Him.

debates.question: Is 'You have redeemed me' in verse 5 a past event, or a confident promise of what God will do?

views.label: A past act of God
views.case: The Hebrew verb is in the perfect tense, and the natural sense is that the LORD has redeemed David before, so the prayer rests on remembered rescues. The same sort of memory appears in verse 21, where the LORD 'has shown me His loving devotion in a city under siege'.

views.label: A confident future
views.case: A perfect tense can express a certainty so firm that it is spoken as done. Read so, David commits his spirit because he is sure of the redemption that is coming, and the verse stands as an act of faith in things not yet seen.

views.label: Both, because the redemption is one continuing work
views.case: The word describes the LORD's habit of rescuing His own, seen in the past and expected again. A man may commit his spirit into hands that have already held him.

debates.bearing: On any reading the verse joins present trust to remembered faithfulness. Jesus quotes only the first half and leaves the words 'You have redeemed me' unspoken. The redemption on His lips is the one He is about to accomplish for others, by His death, and confirm by rising.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1's 'taken refuge' is chasah, a verb of trust that carries the picture of running for shelter, and it comes back in verse 19 when the goodness stored up is for 'those who take refuge in You'. The psalm thus opens and closes its central sections with the same word, first as David's act and then as the LORD's provision for all who do it. Beside it stands batach, to trust or lean on, in verse 6 and verse 14, and the two words together give the psalm's full vocabulary for reliance.

The verb in 'I commit my spirit' is afqid, a form of paqad, whose noun is the word for a deposit left in someone's keeping, as in Genesis 41:36, where it names the grain laid up against the famine. David is depositing his life with God for safekeeping. The Greek Old Testament renders the verb with a word for placing something in another's charge, and that is the verb Luke gives to Jesus, and Peter uses in 1 Peter 4:19, where believers are told to entrust their souls to a faithful Creator. In verse 5 the word for what is deposited is ruach, the breath or spirit, so the request is for God to hold the very breath of life.

The verb 'redeemed' is padah, which means to ransom or set free at a cost, the word used in Exodus 13 for redeeming the firstborn. The Hebrew perfect tense, as the debate on this verse notes, can be heard as a past act or a settled confidence. God is addressed as 'God of truth', emet, meaning reliable and firm, the opposite of the lies of verse 6 and of the slander in verse 13.

Verse 6 has a textual difficulty that the BSB footnote records: the Hebrew says 'I hate', and one Hebrew manuscript with the Greek and the Syriac has 'You hate'. The phrase 'worthless idols' is literally the vapours of emptiness, and it is the same phrase found in Jonah 2:8. The Hebrew for the idols is hevel, the word that gives Ecclesiastes its refrain, breath or vapour.

The contrast between narrow and broad drives the psalm's imagery. The 'distress' of verse 9 is from a root meaning narrow, tight, or to be squeezed. The 'open' of verse 8 is a word meaning a broad or roomy place, which is used for deliverance in Psalm 18:19 and 118:5. The man who was wedged into a tight corner is set on a wide plain.

In verse 16 'make Your face shine' is the language of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:25, and verse 21 places 'loving devotion', chesed, in a city under siege. The phrase may mean a fortified city, and it can also mean a city hemmed in by an army. The 'alarm' of verse 22 is a word for haste and panic, and the same noun stands in Psalm 116:11, 'In my alarm I said, "All men are liars!"' Speech made in panic, in both psalms, is later corrected by the LORD's answer. Finally, 'be strong and courageous' in verse 24 uses the pair chazaq and amats, the charge given to Joshua, and the 'hope' that follows is yachal, a word for waiting with expectation, which recurs in Psalm 33:18 and 33:22.

typology.fulfillment: David entrusted his spirit to God in a time of mortal danger, and Jesus takes the same sentence to the cross, Luke 23:46. The correspondence is exact in wording, with the one addition of 'Father'. The escalation is that David spoke it hoping for rescue from death, while Jesus spoke it in the act of dying, knowing that His Father would raise Him, Acts 2:24. Stephen then prays a version of the same prayer at his death, Acts 7:59, and Peter tells suffering believers to entrust their souls to their faithful Creator, 1 Peter 4:19. The type is exceeded because Jesus' commitment of His spirit is the ground on which every believer may commit theirs.

David is 'dreaded by my friends', who 'flee when they see me on the street'. In Gethsemane, when the soldiers seized Jesus, 'everyone deserted Him and fled', Mark 14:50. The abandonment of the righteous sufferer by those closest to him is the correspondence. The escalation is that Jesus bore the desertion in silence, and in His prayer on the cross He did not curse those who fled but entrusted Himself to the Father who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. The type falls short in that David's flight was a matter of stigma, while the disciples' flight came after they had sworn to stay.

typology.type: The conspiracy to take a life, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The enemies 'conspire against me and plot to take my life'. Matthew records that when morning came, 'all the chief priests and elders of the people conspired against Jesus to put Him to death', Matthew 27:1, and John says that from the day of the raising of Lazarus they planned to kill Him, John 11:53. The parallel of slander, terror and plotted execution is close. The type is escalated because Jesus was not delivered from the plot but through it, and the cross became the very place where God's purpose was accomplished, Acts 2:23-24.

typology.type: Goodness laid up, the secret place of God's presence, verses 19 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The psalm describes a store of goodness kept for those who fear God, and a hiding place in His presence far from human schemes. Paul says of believers, 'your life is now hidden with Christ in God', Colossians 3:3, and Peter speaks of an inheritance 'reserved in heaven for you', 1 Peter 1:4. The shelter that David found in God is found, for the believer, in union with the crucified and risen Christ. The type is not yet complete: the goodness is still in store, and its full display waits for the day when what is hidden is revealed.

study.christ:
The most direct link is Luke 23:46. Luke does not treat the psalm as a text to be proved but as the language in which Jesus died. He gives it as the last word before His breath leaves Him, and the observation that the centurion glorified God follows at once. Jesus quotes the first half of the verse and adds the address 'Father'. This tells us something about how He read the Psalter: as the prayer book of a Son speaking to His Father, and as a book whose words He could fill to the full.

He leaves out the second half of the verse, 'You have redeemed me', and there is a fitting reason. The redemption is the very thing He is accomplishing at that moment. David could say it looking back. Jesus says the first half and goes on to do the second. The Father's raising of Him, Acts 2:24, is the answer to the whole psalm's petition that God should not let the righteous be put to shame, verse 1. Peter preaches that 'God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death', and that answer stands as God's verdict on the trust that the psalm commends.

The psalm's portrait of the sufferer in verses 9 to 13 also fits Him closely, though the New Testament does not lean on it with formal citation. Friends flee, Mark 14:50, rulers conspire, Matthew 27:1, the slander of many is heard, and He is treated as a man forgotten. The correspondence is best taken as an echo and a pattern. It shows the passion as the fullest form of a kind of suffering that the righteous had known before, and it explains why the early church could hear their Lord's voice in the Psalter. Peter draws on the same texture when he says that Jesus 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly', 1 Peter 2:23.

The psalm's answer to distress, the shelter and the goodness laid up, points to Christ as the place of hiding. Paul says that the believer's life is hidden with Christ in God, Colossians 3:3, and the man who took refuge in verse 1 has a true refuge in the One who was cast out in his place. The 'open' place of verse 8 is the free place Christ brings believers to, in the freedom He gives, Galatians 5:1.

The 'hour' theme adds one more strand. 'My times are in Your hands' is the confession of one whose life is ordered by another. John shows Jesus moving toward His hour, which was not yet come in John 7:30 and had come at John 13:1. He does so not as a victim of events but as one whose times were in His Father's hands.

The reading should not be forced. Verses 6 and 17 to 18 are David's and are not put on Jesus' lips. Verse 10 speaks of iniquity, and Jesus had none. What is fulfilled in Christ is the pattern of trusting entrustment, and He is at once the one who prays the psalm most perfectly and the reason those who pray it may hope.
study.god:
This psalm shows a God who is a place before He is a rescuer. The opening images are all of security: rock, fortress, stronghold, refuge. Only after several verses does the psalm ask for rescue. The God of the psalm is the one who is safe to run to, and the running comes first. That is why the trust can be spoken while the enemies are still at the door.

He is a God who sees. 'You have seen my affliction; You have known the anguish of my soul', verse 7. The verbs are seeing and knowing, and the object is the interior life. God knows not only what happened to David but what it was like. It is a truth the psalm holds against the temptation of verse 22, where David felt cut off from God's sight. The psalm corrects the feeling: he was never out of sight.

He is a God of truth, emet, and this shapes the psalm's moral atmosphere. Around David are lying lips and arrogant contempt, verses 13 and 18, and the idols of verse 6 are a lie. Against them stands the God who does not deceive. The Lord who redeems is also the Lord who repays: 'The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant', verse 23. That is justice, held with no anxiety, and David is content to leave it to God, verse 15.

He is generous beyond what is asked. David begs to be kept from shame and to be hidden, and the psalm goes on to speak of goodness that God has 'laid up' for the fearful and 'bestowed before the sons of men', verse 19. The gifts are plentiful and are put on display. The God of the psalm keeps treasure for His people and shows it in public.

He holds time. The confession 'My times are in Your hands', verse 15, says that the seasons of a life, its birth and death and every reversal between, are under a hand that is good. It is a strong doctrine of providence, and it is a comfort because the hand belongs to the God whose face shines on His servant, verse 16, and not to fate.

For worship the psalm teaches us to say the deposit prayer at night and at death. It gives us the words to commit ourselves to God in the smallest and largest crises. It teaches us to love the LORD, verse 23, and not only to fear or use Him, and it reminds a congregation that the strength to be courageous does not come from ourselves. It comes from the fact that the LORD preserves the faithful.

crossReferences.note: The opening of Psalm 71 repeats the opening of this psalm almost word for word, from taking refuge in the LORD and asking never to be put to shame, to the appeal to be a rock of refuge and a fortress. It shows that these were shared prayers, taught and reused by the worshipping community, and that David's private trust was handed on as a liturgy.

Luke sets the darkness over the land and the torn temple veil before the final cry, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit'. Jesus takes verse 5 as the language for His last breath, and the fact that Luke ends the scene there shows that the psalm was understood as the right form of words for dying into the care of God.

Stephen, dying under the stones of his accusers, prays, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit'. The prayer copies Jesus' own use of verse 5, addressed now to Jesus Himself. It shows the first martyr following his Lord in the use of the psalm and treating Jesus as the one into whose hands a spirit may be committed.

Believers who suffer according to God's will are told to entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and keep doing good. The verb of entrusting is the same idea as verse 5's commitment. Peter turns the psalm's prayer into a standing habit for the persecuted church, and grounds it in the faithfulness of God as Creator.

Jeremiah hears the whispering of many, 'Terror is on every side!', from friends who watch for his fall. The phrase and the situation match verse 13 and verse 11. The prophet then goes on to praise the LORD as a warrior at his side, so that the experience of being slandered and abandoned is again turned into trust.

Jonah, praying from the belly of the fish, says that those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion. The wording is the same as verse 6, and it shows how the phrase had become a stock way of contrasting empty gods with the God who saves, in a prayer that ends with the confession that salvation belongs to the LORD.

The priestly blessing asks that the LORD cause His face to shine upon His people. Verse 16 makes the same request in a personal form, 'Make Your face shine on Your servant'. The link shows that David's prayer is rooted in the promise Israel heard at every blessing, and that the face of God is the source of all safety.

The psalmist says, 'In my alarm I said, "All men are liars!"'. The word for alarm is the same as in verse 22, where David said, 'I am cut off from Your sight!' In both psalms panic speaks a false verdict, and the answer of God shows the speech to have been hasty. The pair helps believers own their worst thoughts without being ruled by them.

David calls on his hearers to wait for the LORD and be strong and courageous, and the wording is echoed in verse 24. Both psalms end with the same charge, and both are prayed in a threatened situation. Together they show that courage in Scripture is the fruit of waiting on God, not a temperament.

God commands Joshua to be strong and courageous, not afraid or discouraged, because the LORD goes with him. Verse 24 gives that command to every believer, not only a leader. The reason is the same in each: courage is possible because God is present, and the psalm applies to ordinary sufferers a charge first given at the threshold of the land.

Paul says believers have died and their life is now hidden with Christ in God. The verse reads like the fulfilment of the secret place of God's presence in verse 20, where the faithful are concealed from the schemes of men. It gives the psalm's image its New Testament home in union with Christ.

When Jesus was abused He did not retaliate, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. The verse shows the spirit in which Jesus prayed this psalm: He left judgment to the Father, as David does in verses 15 and 23, and it tells the reader that the commitment of verse 5 includes the commitment of one's cause.

study.oneStory:
From the first chapters of Genesis, the human story has been one of fear and hiding. The man and woman hid among the trees when they heard God walking in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and their descendants have gone on looking for shelters, some in God and many in idols. This psalm is a strong statement of the alternative. It says that the only shelter that holds is the LORD, that idols are vapour, and that a person may run to God even when he is guilty and ashamed. The scene of Genesis 3, in which God comes seeking, and the psalm's confession that God has seen affliction, belong to one picture.

The psalm also gathers what Israel had learned since. God met Abraham with the words 'Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield', Genesis 15:1. He met Israel at the sea with the message 'Do not be afraid', and He met Joshua with 'Be strong and courageous'. David's charge in verse 24 calls the whole people to take their place in that line. The story of Israel is a story of a people hemmed in, from Egypt through the wilderness to the exile, and of God setting their feet in a spacious place again and again. It is also the story of a king pursued by his own people, so that even the anointed one knew the desertion of friends.

The plot reaches its centre when the greater Son of David goes to the cross in the same trust. Jesus is betrayed by a friend, deserted by the twelve, slandered before the council, and He commits His spirit to the Father, Luke 23:46. The Father raises Him, and in that act the redemption of verse 5 is shown to be real and not merely hoped for. The disciples who fled find the one who had entrusted Himself to His Father come back to them, alive. The church then takes the same prayer on its lips, from Stephen on.

The story ends in the place the psalm names. The 'secret place of Your presence' becomes the city in which God dwells with His people, where they see His face, Revelation 22:4. What David saw as stored goodness is then poured out, the schemes and slanders and accusing tongues are silent, and the fear that his life was cut off from God's sight is answered forever. The command of the last verse, 'Be strong and courageous', is given to a people who have not yet arrived, and the ending explains why they can obey it. The LORD preserves the faithful, and He will bring them home.

sermon.title: "My Times Are in Your Hand" - Part One (Biola)
sermon.why: Begg preaches on Psalm 31:15, showing that to say 'my times are in Your hand' means we are not trapped by blind fate or tossed about by chance, but are being schooled in the providence of a God who is making us like His Son.

quiz.q: What does David commit into God's hands in verse 5, and who later prays these exact words?

options.text: His spirit; Jesus prays these words while dying on the cross, Luke 23:46.
options.note: This is the psalm's central confession and its direct New Testament fulfillment.

options.text: His spirit; Stephen later echoes similar words while being stoned, Acts 7:59.
options.note: Close, since Stephen does pray something similar as he dies, but the psalm's words are quoted verbatim by Jesus Himself, Luke 23:46, which is the direct fulfillment in view here.

options.text: His kingdom; Solomon later prays this at the temple dedication.
options.note: The verse is about David's own spirit, not his kingdom, and is fulfilled by Jesus, not Solomon.

options.text: His army; Joshua later prays this before battle.
options.note: The verse concerns committing one's spirit at the point of vulnerability, not military strategy.

quiz.q: How does David describe his experience among his friends in verse 11?

options.text: He is dreaded by his friends, who flee when they see him in the street.
options.note: This verse describes painful abandonment even by those closest to him.

options.text: His friends grow distant and stop visiting, though they do not actively flee.
options.note: Close, since growing distance is part of the picture, but the verse describes something more dramatic, friends fleeing at the very sight of him in the street.

options.text: His friends betray him but never physically avoid him.
options.note: The text specifically describes friends fleeing at the sight of him in the street, more than passive betrayal.

options.text: He has no friends to speak of at all.
options.note: The verse implies he did have friends, who then dreaded and avoided him, not that he never had any.

quiz.q: What confession does David make in verse 14 despite his distress?

options.text: "But I trust in You, O LORD; I say, 'You are my God.'"
options.note: This marks the psalm's renewed confession of trust in the middle of ongoing distress.

options.text: "I hope God is still with me, though I am not certain."
options.note: Close in tone, since the psalm includes real uncertainty elsewhere, but verse 14 itself is a direct, confident confession, 'You are my God,' not a tentative hope.

options.text: "I will seek help from foreign gods instead."
options.note: David explicitly rejects worthless idols elsewhere in the psalm, verse 6, and reaffirms trust in the LORD alone.

options.text: "I demand that God explain my suffering."
options.note: The verse is a confession of trust, not a demand for explanation.

quiz.q: What does verse 15 say about David's times?

options.text: They are in God's hands.
options.note: This phrase grounds David's confidence that his circumstances, not just his spirit, are held securely by God.

options.text: They are generally watched over by God, though not specifically controlled by Him.
options.note: Close, since God's care is the point, but the verse states directly and specifically that David's times 'are in Your hands,' active possession, not general, hands-off watching.

options.text: They are determined by his enemies.
options.note: The verse specifically attributes control to God, even though enemies and pursuers are mentioned in the same breath.

options.text: They are entirely unknown even to God.
options.note: The verse affirms God's active possession of David's times, not divine ignorance of them.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's closing exhortation in verse 24?

options.text: Be strong and courageous, all who hope in the LORD.
options.note: The psalm ends by extending its personal testimony into an exhortation for the whole community of faith.

options.text: Be patient and calm, without any call to active courage.
options.note: Close, since patience is implied by hoping in the LORD, but verse 24 explicitly calls for active strength and courage, not merely passive calm.

options.text: Seek vengeance personally against all enemies.
options.note: The psalm prays for God's justice against the wicked, verses 17-18, but the closing exhortation is about courage and hope, not personal vengeance.

options.text: Withdraw from community and suffer alone.
options.note: The exhortation addresses 'all who hope in the LORD,' a communal call, not a call to isolation.

questions: David commits his very spirit into God's hands, words Jesus later prayed while dying. What would it mean for you to entrust not just your circumstances but your very life into God's hands today?
David experiences the pain of friends fleeing from him in his distress. Have you ever felt abandoned by people you expected to stand by you, and how did that shape your trust in God?
Despite deep distress, David renews his confession, 'You are my God,' and declares that his times are in God's hands. What present uncertainty in your life most needs this same renewed confession?

Jesus's use of this psalm's words on the cross shows that even His darkest hour was held within a psalm of trust, not despair alone. How does knowing Jesus prayed these very words change how you read your own hardest prayers?
The psalm closes urging all who hope in the LORD to be strong and courageous. Where do you need that courage this week, and who around you might also need to hear this exhortation from you?

translationNotes.note: Into Your hands I commit my spirit was used in later Jewish tradition as an evening prayer of committal before sleep, and is quoted by Jesus without alteration as His last words from the cross, Luke 23:46.
Cut off from Your sight reflects a moment of despair within the psalm, immediately answered by the testimony that God heard his plea, showing that feelings of abandonment are not the final word.
